headword: Lady Macbeth. O, eile! Eile her! damit ich meinen Geist in deinen giesse, durch meine tapfere Zunge diese Zweifel und Furchtgespenster aus dem Felde schlage, die dich wegschrecken von dem goldnen Reif, womit das Glück dich gern bekrönen möchte.
line: The scene can be interpreted as follows. Having read Macbeth’s letter describing the witches’ prophecy, Lady Macbeth sees that her husband is “too kind to resolve to become king”. She decides to take on the task of pouring that resolve into him and driving out his hesitation through words. Here, “Geist” (“spirit”) means courage, boldness, and the ability to make ruthless decisions, while “tapfere Zunge” (“valiant tongue”) shows her awareness of the power of manipulative language as a weapon. “Goldner Reif” (“golden circlet”) is an indirect expression for the crown, while “Glück” (“fortune” or “luck”) can also be read as a perilous turn of phrase that presents the temptation to sin as though it were fate’s blessing.

Characteristics and role: Incorporating research and information about the works that followed the publication of Müller von Asow's catalogue, this catalogue reorganized the works as a whole in order of composition (chronological order). Its chronological arrangement (from the earliest studies of 1870 to the final works of 1949) is useful for tracing the development of Richard Strauss's creative activity and establishing and identifying dates of composition. The Richard-Strauss-Quellenverzeichnis (Richard Strauss Sources Catalogue / RSQV) takes TrV as its starting point and corrects and supplements the information about the works. TrV is also referenced in research and scholarly editions such as Richard Strauss Werke. Kritische Ausgabe (the critical edition of Richard Strauss's works), although information based on either catalogue may require correction in the light of subsequent research.

Thus, the catalogues differ in their origins and organization: an earlier, detailed thematic catalogue (AV), followed by a catalogue (TrV) that reorganized the works as a whole chronologically in light of subsequent research. However, AV also uses chronological ordering within its categories, and versions of TrV from 1993 onward also contain thematic incipits. They are consulted as complementary resources, and there are examples of both numbers appearing together in the official list of works.

As an expressive direction, it indicates simplicity or an unadorned manner. In the GM entries, it means “simple” or “plain.” When accompanied by ohne Sentimentalität or ohne Pathos, it also calls for the avoidance of sentimentality or exaggerated emotion.

In the GM entries, the present participle einhaltend directs the performers to hold back and ease the music’s forward movement, and is translated as “slacken the tempo.” In stage directions, it can also mean to stop playing or pause in an action. The wording and surrounding context show what is to be maintained, what action is to stop, or what movement is to be checked.

The related noun Einhalt is used in the expressions Einhalt tun and Einhalt gebieten, meaning “to stop” or “to put a check on.” It is not simply an inflected form of einhalten, but searches for examples from this entry also include occurrences of this noun.

Mit Empfindung means “with feeling” (con sentimento), or “with deeply felt emotion.” In the GM examples, Empfindung is rendered in Japanese with a word meaning “feeling”. In RS, mit Empfindung is also translated as “with feeling”.
Adjective, also used adverbially. Comparative energischer; superlative am energischsten.

The related verb entfernen means “to remove,” while the reflexive form sich entfernen means “to move away” or “to leave.” Entfernend is its present participle. These are not inflected forms of the noun Entfernung, but searches for examples from this entry also include these verbal forms.

The related noun Entschluss (older spelling Entschluß) means “resolution” or “decision.” It is not simply an inflected form of entschlossen, but searches for examples from this entry also include occurrences of this noun.

In [RS: Till], it appears as an expressive direction attached to a clarinet phrase. In stage directions, it can also describe a person’s appearance: in Tannhäuser in [RW: Oper], sein Antlitz ist bleich und entstellt is translated as “his face is pale and haggard.”
The related noun Entzücken means “delight,” “joy,” or “rapture.” It is not simply an inflected form of entzückt, but searches for examples from this entry also include occurrences of this noun.
In stage directions, it may also mean “seized” or “captured.”
Depending on the context, it can also suggest agitation tinged with impatience.
The past participle of “erreichen.” It also has the same form as the present tense in expressions such as “er erreicht” (“he reaches”).

In GM, I translate this as “as though dying,” although “fading away” would also work. GM also uses morendo in many passages, alongside ersterbend. Personally, I feel an emotional, introspective nuance in ersterbend, whereas morendo (which also derives from morire, “to die”) suggests “moving towards silence” or “fading away naturally.” I wonder what difference in nuance Mahler himself felt between them.

In performance directions, etwas modifies an adjective or adverb to temper its degree, and is translated as “somewhat,” “a little,” or similar expressions. In stage directions, it can also express a small difference in distance or position.
For stage action, sense ② can be rendered as “to move swiftly.” Zurückfahren means “to recoil,” and fortfahren means “to continue.” Fahren lassen can also mean “to let go” or “to abandon.”

For a composition, Fassung means a version or draft. It may refer to a revised version of an opera, for example, or a translated version of a vocal text. “A revised version” can be expressed as “revidierte Fassung,” but the context may also allow Fassung alone to refer to a particular revision or draft.

In addition to being a comparative meaning “farther” or an inflected adjective, ferner is also used as an adverb meaning “furthermore” or “in addition.” Searches for examples from this entry also include this adverbial usage.

The noun Feste means “fortress” or “stronghold” and is distinct from feste, an inflected form of the adjective fest. Searches for examples from this entry also include occurrences of this identically spelled noun.

Adjective, also used adverbially. The comparative is finsterer or finstrer and the superlative am finstersten. Inflected forms include finstere or finstre, finsteres or finstres, and finsterem or finstrem.

Adjective, also used adverbially. Comparative freundlicher; superlative am freundlichsten. Freundlichem, freundlichen and freundlicher can be inflected attributive forms.
② Well-disposed or amicable; also pleasant, cheerful or inviting, as of weather, rooms or colours.

English: As soon as the night watchman’s horn sounds (3/4 time), the women pour strong streams of water from jugs, pitchers and basins out of all the windows onto those fighting below. This, together with the particularly powerful sound of the horn, strikes everyone with panic. Neighbours, apprentices, craftsmen and masters flee in haste in all directions, so that the stage is very soon completely empty. The house doors are hurriedly shut; the female neighbours also disappear from the windows, slamming them shut.

The degree of separation and emphasis depends on the instrument and the surrounding directions. The passage above also carries the marking p marcato. Strong articulation does not necessarily mean a loud dynamic.

The word can also refer to octave notation. The prime sign (′) placed to the upper right of a note name is called a Strich (stroke); the number of these strokes indicates which octave the note belongs to. For example, dreimal gestrichenes C means “three-line C”.

There are also examples such as breit gestrichen, kurz gestrichen, and lang gestrichen that describe the breadth or length of the bow stroke. For example, breit gestrichen is translated here as “With broad bow strokes” and kurz gestrichen as “With short bow strokes”.

In the GM example at bar 860 of SYMPHONIE III, movement I, this means rolling a cymbal (with a sponge-headed mallet). In GM, it is translated as “stridently”, “shrilly”, and similar expressions. For instructions concerning the voice in RW and RS, “in a shrieking voice” may also be suitable.

It has many meanings and is difficult to translate. In GM, mit großem Ton and similar expressions are translated as “with a full tone”. “With a grand tone” or “with a powerful sound” might also be suitable.
It also appears to have the meaning “root (in harmony).” Ralph Dunstan’s music dictionary defines Grund as a “fundamental note, generator,” among other meanings.
Half; partial; incomplete. eine halbe Stunde means “half an hour”; the noun denoting the thing halved can also be omitted.

It can describe lowering the voice out of consideration for others. In singing or speech, suitable renderings include “at half voice” and “with the voice lowered”. a mezza voce is a corresponding expression; sotto voce is also close in its sense of a low or subdued delivery.
Bindebogen generally means “slur”, but is also used more broadly to include a tie joining notes of the same pitch.
Adjective, also used adverbially. Comparative hastiger; superlative am hastigsten.

In GM, it can be used to indicate a return to the principal tempo of the movement or section after changes of tempo within the music. Depending on the context, it can also refer to the basic tempo in contrast to local changes of speed, rather than necessarily to the tempo at the very beginning.

The following is a guide to servants, attendants, and domestic workers in RS’s Der Rosenkavalier Op.59. Even the same terms—Diener, Lakai, and Livree—can have substantially different functions depending on whose household they belong to. It is therefore useful to distinguish the Marschallin’s household, Faninal’s household, Baron Ochs’s entourage, and the inn staff. Octavian’s own attendants, who appear in Act II, must also be distinguished. Since differentiating every term in translation would become extremely cumbersome, some are grouped together on the search page.

The group of footmen serving in the Marschallin’s residence. In Act I, they try to prevent Baron Ochs from forcing his way in and guard the boundary between the bedroom and the antechamber. During the morning reception, they also open and close doors, move furniture, organize visitors, and coordinate the movements of the Friseur, Sänger, and others.

【Rank: middle to lower / servants in a great aristocratic residence】They belong to a separate organization from servants of the Faninal household and Baron Ochs’s attendants. They show that the Marschallin’s residence, although the setting is her private bedroom, is also a highly organized aristocratic space.

A lower-ranking footman in a residence. Responsible for miscellaneous duties such as opening and closing doors, showing visitors in, and running errands; he is often also stationed for ceremonial purposes or visual effect.

【Rank: special (low)】He carries the case for the silver rose, accompanies the Baron to his secret rendezvous at the inn, and tries to clear a path for the Baron’s departure near the end. He is also implied to be the Baron’s illegitimate son and visually conveys the private, disorderly domestic arrangements of the Lerchenau household.
Example searches from this entry also include uses of the related adjective heilig (“holy”).
Adjective, also used adverbially. Comparative heller; superlative am hellsten.
Adverb, also used as a separable particle with verbs of movement.

Masculine noun (der Herd). Genitive singular des Herdes / des Herds; nominative plural die Herde; dative plural den Herden.Herde can also be a literary dative singular. The feminine noun Herde (herd or flock) is a different word.

In performance directions, it describes bringing a line, especially a melody, into relief or to the fore. In GM, it is translated as “bring out”. In stage directions in [RW: Oper], [RS: Oper], and similar sources, it can also mean “stepping forward into the foreground of the stage”.

The Hess catalogue was not compiled simply to classify works without opus numbers. It catalogues works and materials omitted from the old Beethoven complete edition published by Breitkopf & Härtel in the nineteenth century. It therefore includes not only independent, completed works but also first versions, alternative versions, arrangements and reworkings, unfinished works, fragments, sketches, and composition exercises. Hess numbers can also be assigned to alternative versions or arrangements of works that have opus or WoO numbers, so the Hess, Op., and WoO systems are not mutually exclusive.

Whereas WoO numbers are used to classify works without opus numbers, Hess numbers are supplementary catalogue numbers for works and creative materials omitted from the old complete edition. The two catalogues have different inclusion criteria, and neither simply contains the other. The Hess catalogue includes completed works as well as alternative versions, arrangements and reworkings, unfinished works, fragments, sketches, and composition exercises; WoO also includes unfinished works.
③ A canopy of fabric or similar material; also a vehicle’s roof lining.
Directional adverb, invariable, with no normal comparative or superlative. Also used as a separable verbal prefix, often more literary than hinunter.

An abbreviation for the catalogue of Joseph Haydn's works (Hoboken-Verzeichnis) compiled by the Dutch musicologist Anthony van Hoboken. Works are classified by genre and identified by a Roman-numeral group number followed by a number within that group. For example, Symphony No. 100 in G major is Hob. I:100. An overview of groups I–XXXI is given below; subsidiary categories such as Ia are omitted. There is also a group XXXII for pasticcios (works assembled from pre-existing pieces).
Third-person singular present of horchen; the same form also serves as the second-person plural present and imperative.

In GM, immer can indicate continuation of an earlier manner of playing or an existing state, as in “Immer ff” (“Continue ff.”) and “immer am Steg” (“Continue playing near the bridge.”). The term is also frequently used with a comparative in sense ②.
When describing tone colour, it can also be rendered as “with an intense tone colour”.
① Arousing pity; pitiable, distressing, or lamentable. Also plaintive or expressing helpless distress or fear.

A related musical work is Claude Debussy’s Golliwogg’s Cake-walk. It is the sixth piece in the suite Children’s Corner, and the Golliwogg in its title refers to a rag doll caricaturing a Black person. The figure became widely known through a picture book published in 1895 and illustrated by Florence Kate Upton, and was also popular as a children’s toy. Its features, including its black face, large eyes and exaggerated lips, are connected with the imagery of contemporary minstrel shows, in which performers blackened their faces to portray Black people, and embody racial stereotypes.

The cakewalk is a dance that developed among enslaved Black people in America. One aspect of it involved imitating and satirizing the affected gestures and dances of the white upper classes. Its name derives from the practice of awarding a cake to the winner of a dance competition. It later spread through Europe and America as a form of stage entertainment and was also incorporated into Debussy’s music. In Golliwogg’s Cake-walk, both the dance and the doll bring together the reception of Black culture and representations of Black people at the time.
Debussy also composed a separate short piano piece using cakewalk rhythms, Le petit nègre (the little Black person).

In the Glockenspiel part in the first movement of Mahler's SYMPHONIE VII, the instruction "mit Klöppeln" appears and is translated there as “with mallets”. From a modern perspective, however, playing the Glockenspiel “with mallets” is a matter of course. Yet the “keyboard glockenspiel (Tastenglockenspiel)” was also in use in GM's time, and it is highly likely that SYMPHONIE VII likewise presupposes a keyboard glockenspiel (for example, the aria No.20 in Mozart's “The Magic Flute” (Bärenreiter p.258) bears the designation "Strumento d'acciaio (Glockenspiel)" (“instrument of steel”) and contains many multiple-note combinations and rapid passages, making it highly likely that a keyboard glockenspiel was intended). In that light, an instruction to play with “mallets” rather than a “keyboard” makes sense.

Neuter noun (das Knie). Genitive singular des Knies; nominative plural die Knie; dative plural den Knien. The corpus also uses the older plural spellings Kniee and Knieen.

The suffix “-mäßig” also means “-like”, “in the style of”, “having the character of”, or “suited to”.

● In Der fliegende Holländer WWV 63, the Steuermann is directed to put the Sprachrohr quickly to his mouth and call out over the side of the ship. Elsewhere in the same work, there is also a direction to call out with both hands held to the mouth.

In a later scene, there is also a direction to sing from an opening in the stage floor through a Sprachrohr led to the monster’s mouth from inside. These directions specify the device or route through which the voice passes; specific changes in pitch or timbre need to be considered in light of production documentation and other relevant materials.

“Schlag” can also mean a beat. From its sense of a blow or stroke, it refers in music to an individual beat or conducting stroke. The expression “in one beat (one conducting beat to a bar)” is “In einem Schlag”; it describes the action of giving one conducting beat per bar.

In older German writings and scores, such as those of J. S. Bach, the word may also refer to an instrument’s stops or mechanisms being “in operation (switched on).” In Mahler’s SYMPHONIE II, “1. 2. 3. 4. Horn in F in der Ferne; sind an den in der Partitur bemerkten Stellen mit im Orch. thätig.” describes a rule governing placement: “Horns 1, 2, 3 and 4 in F are placed in the distance, but at the passages indicated in the score, they also take part in the main orchestra’s performance.”

In RS's Die Liebe der Danae Op.83, the score contains six numbered transposition directions. These concern the vocal passages of Jupiter (baritone), Danae (soprano) and Midas (tenor). RS himself is reported to have agreed “quite reluctantly” to transpositions intended to accommodate Jupiter's high tessitura. There have also been performances in which the role of Jupiter was sung in the original key. In performance, besides deciding uniformly for the entire work whether or not to transpose, another possible approach is to make that choice for each Transposition passage according to the singers' vocal ranges. The specific treatment needs to be understood in light of the documentation for each individual production.

In music, it conveys an urgent, forward-driving impetus. Where a change of speed is intended, it may also be rendered “quickening the pace”. AV also arranges works chronologically within groups separated by opus-number status and other categories; TrV places compositions in chronological order across those divisions.

Building on earlier research, this catalogue arranges the works broadly in order of composition, including early works and fragments. Its chronological arrangement surveys Strauss’s output from his early to his late years, making it useful for tracing his creative development and identifying the dates of works. TrV is also used to identify works in Richard Strauss Werke. Kritische Ausgabe and has been adopted as a standard work-number system in library cataloguing.

Flöte” is rendered as “Flute 4 switches to piccolo 2.” The past participle “übernommen” can describe a role or passage being taken by another performer, as in “Alto voice (may also, if appropriate, be taken by a baritone).” In RW, “die Wacht übernommen” means “taken over the watch”. ① Blown or swept away by the wind; covered by windblown sand or snow. Also rendered “as if blown away by the wind”.
② Faded, dispersed or effaced, as of tracks, memories or sounds; of sound, also “fading faintly away”, “as if fading into the distance” or “indistinctly”.
An action may be expressed “outwardly” (including self-directed speech or a low voice), but the phrase need not involve speaking: it can also describe silent reflection or looking ahead.

In Mahler, if “vorwärts” follows “ritardando,” it may be understood as asking the performer to restore the tempo and regain the flow. “With forward motion” or “with renewed impetus” may also be suitable.
Masculine noun (der Wein). Genitive singular des Weins or des Weines; nominative plural die Weine; dative plural den Weinen. Weine also occurs as an older dative singular.
The piano/vocal score of “Trost im Unglück”, however, also contains this phrase.

In GM, the uninflected word “weit” occurs only in the first movement of SYMPHONIE IX, where “so weit … als nötig” is translated as “as much as necessary.” Inflected forms such as “weiter” and “weitester” also occur in other works.

For Robert Schumann, WoO numbers were also used in the earlier catalogue by Kurt Hofmann and Siegmar Keil. However, the principal modern scholarly catalogue, Robert Schumann: Thematisch-Bibliographisches Werkverzeichnis, edited by Margit L. McCorkle and commonly known as the Robert-Schumann-Werkverzeichnis (RSW, 2003), assigns WoO 1–8 to works without opus numbers that Schumann published or prepared for publication, while other fragments, unpublished works, projects and similar materials are classified chiefly in the Anhang (appendix).

WoO numbers are also sometimes used for certain works by Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy in older scores and recording documentation. However, the current standard catalogue, the Mendelssohn-Werkverzeichnis (MWV, 2009), uses its own genre-based numbering system, such as MWV U 136, rather than WoO as its principal formal classification.

Neuter noun (das Wort). Genitive singular des Worts/des Wortes. Wörter usually counts separate words; Worte usually refers to connected utterances or meaningful expressions. Dative plurals are Wörtern and Worten. Worte can also be an old dative singular.
② Powerful, forceful or vigorous; also rendered “with a powerful impact” or “with immense force”.
① Intense anger, rage or indignation; also rendered “with furious anger” or “raging”.
③ Indecisive in taking action; also rendered “with uncertainty”.

In GM, zart is rendered as “delicately” and weich as “softly”, reflecting their combination in zart und weich in movement VI, bar 245 of DAS LIED VON DER ERDE. Depending on context, “tenderly” may also suit zart, while “gracefully” is possible where gracefulness is intended. The meanings of sanft, weich and zart overlap and require choices according to context.
① In sich Zeit lassen, to take one's time, not to hurry or to proceed at leisure; also rendered “allow plenty of time” or “at leisure”.

English: Note: The stage band must be placed at a considerable distance from the stage here. Nevertheless, the individual entries must be played very loudly, to create the effect of the din of battle being carried over in intermittent gusts of wind. Each entry must therefore also be accompanied by gusting-wind sound effects.
Depending on the operatic context, “in a sharp whisper,” “spitting the words out,” or “with a sharply rasping voice” may also work.
In Wagner’s Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg, Zorn also occurs as a character’s name. In these passages, it is a proper name rather than the common noun meaning “anger”.
Both RW and RS contain examples of sense ④. In musical contexts, the word can also denote:
② Also; equally or at the same time in another respect.

In GM, this is translated as “with sharp tonguing.” Some interpret it in the fifth movement of Mahler’s SYMPHONIE II as “flutter-tonguing.” Since GM explicitly writes “Flatterzunge” elsewhere, I have translated it here as “with sharp tonguing.” However, around bar 402 of the fifth movement, “Zungenstoss” or its abbreviation appears above notes bearing three tremolo strokes, so the precise playing technique still needs to be checked. Still, I think it unlikely that GM, who was also an excellent conductor and thoroughly familiar with the playing techniques of each instrument, would have requested flutter-tonguing from the reed instruments, on which that technique is difficult. I suspect that he was asking for an “extreme” form of tonguing beyond the standard technique; nevertheless, the passage is very loud, and part of me wonders whether there is really any need to work oneself into a frenzy over it.

In GM, it is used mainly where the tempo becomes slower than before, so I have translated it as “slowing down.” I wonder whether simply translating it as “slowly” is slightly inaccurate. If anything, I feel that “ritenuto” may be more appropriate than “rallentando” or “ritardando.” In stage directions in RW and RS, it can also mean “reservedly,” “restraining someone,” or “with restraint.”
English: Note for the conductor and singer: Here the symbol 𝄐 indicates only a brief pause at the barline, not a fermata (Mahler’s note).
English: With a slight pause.
“To hold back (the tempo)”; “to restrain (ritenuto)”; “to pause”; “to sustain (a note).”

In GM, anhalten is rendered as “slower”; in RW, as “with a pause,” among other translations. It can describe holding back or momentarily stopping something already in motion. In musical contexts, its nuance can be close to the Italian ritenuto (slower; restrained), firmly holding the tempo back at that moment.

The noun Anhalten is rendered here as “a pause.” A footnote to Mahler's Das himmlische Leben, a setting of a poem from Des Knaben Wunderhorn, reads “𝄐 bedeutet hier nur ein kurzes Anhalten auf dem Taktstrich und nicht etwa eine Fermate.” In the GM entry, this passage is translated as “Here the symbol 𝄐 indicates only a brief pause at the barline, not a fermata”.

English: A herald enters the stage, and a trumpeter at his side sounds a long-held note. Adriano and Irene have already stepped aside. The inhabitants rush out of every house, so that the whole square as far as the Lateran Basilica is suddenly covered by a great crowd, which fills it with the most joyful tumult.

English: Inside the donkey driver's hut, very modest but neatly kept. A large bed, a low table with seats, and many colourful cloths in Eastern style. An old carpet hangs across the doorway. Bright sunlight streams in everywhere, through the open window and the hanging at the entrance.
